# Prep DV2 Data

This dataset is going to be the entire master set not filtered by post-secondary completion. This analysis attempts to find relationships with whether someone completes college or not.

```{r}

master.model.dv2 <- master %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2010,
         grad.year <= 2019,
         ps.grad != "Attending ps") %>%
  select(PersonID, all_of(final_ivs)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pseo.participant)) %>%
  mutate(ps.grad = ifelse(ps.grad == "Y", "Yes", "No"),
         ps.grad = fct_relevel(ps.grad, "No"),
         Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
         RaceEthnicity = fct_relevel(RaceEthnicity, "White"),
         economic.status = as_factor(economic.status),
         economic.status = fct_relevel(economic.status, "0"),
         SpecialEdStatus = as.character(SpecialEdStatus),
         SpecialEdStatus = fct_relevel(SpecialEdStatus, "0"),
         english.learner = as_factor(english.learner),
         english.learner = fct_relevel(english.learner, "0"),
         non.english.home = as_factor(non.english.home),
         non.english.home = fct_relevel(non.english.home, "0"),
         Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Entirely rural"),
         edr = fct_relevel(edr, "EDR 1 - Northwest"),
         pseo.participant = as.character(pseo.participant),
         pseo.participant = fct_relevel(pseo.participant, "0"),
         took.ACT = fct_relevel(took.ACT, "No"),
         ACTCompositeScore.filled = ifelse(is.na(ACTCompositeScore), 0, ACTCompositeScore),
         ap.exam = as_factor(ap.exam),
         ap.exam = fct_relevel(ap.exam, "0"),
         cte.achievement = fct_relevel(cte.achievement, "No CTE"))


```

# Modeling - college completion, full population

## Model 1: Demographics

This baseline model examines whether demographic characteristics are associated with postsecondary completion (ps.grad), modeled across the full graduating cohort regardless of postsecondary attendance. N = 34,705.

**Special education status and economic status show the largest demographic associations in this model.** Students with special education status have roughly **73 percent lower odds** of completing postsecondary education than those without (OR = 0.267, p \< .001) — the largest single effect in this model. Economically disadvantaged students have roughly **61 percent lower odds** of completion (OR = 0.393, p \< .001), also a substantial effect.

**Race/ethnicity shows several large and significant disparities, with one category standing out sharply.** Relative to White students, **American Indian students have roughly 63 percent lower odds** of completion (OR = 0.371, p \< .001), **Black students roughly 46 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.543, p \< .001), and **Hispanic students roughly 43 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.575, p \< .001). **Students in the Unknown race/ethnicity category show an extreme disparity** — roughly **92 percent lower odds** of completion (OR = 0.085, p \< .001) — by far the largest effect of any variable in this model, consistent with the unusually low bachelor's attainment this same category showed in the earlier bivariate credential-level analysis. **Asian/PI students show a smaller, only marginally significant disparity** (OR = 0.823, p = .087).

**Gender shows a substantial association in the opposite direction from the other demographic disparities.** Women have roughly **64 percent higher odds** of completing postsecondary education than men (OR = 1.639, p \< .001) — the only variable in this model associated with higher, rather than lower, odds of completion.

**English learner status is associated with lower odds of completion** (OR = 0.578, p \< .001), while **non-English home language shows no significant association** (OR = 0.998, p = .982) once English learner status is accounted for separately — suggesting the language-related barrier to completion is better captured by English learner status specifically, rather than by home language alone.

**Model fit:** AIC = 42,739.24, residual deviance = 42,717 on 34,694 df (null deviance = 48,106 on 34,704 df).

**Summary:** At the demographics-only stage, special education status, economic disadvantage, and race/ethnicity — particularly the sharp disparity in the Unknown race/ethnicity category — show the strongest associations with reduced postsecondary completion, while gender shows a clear, sizable association in the opposite direction, with women considerably more likely to complete than men. These patterns closely mirror the demographic disparities identified in the earlier bivariate work on ps.grad, now confirmed simultaneously in a single model. As high school context and accomplishments are added in subsequent blocks, it will be worth watching whether these associations — especially the very large Unknown race/ethnicity and special education effects — persist, attenuate, or shift once other factors are accounted for.

```{r}
model1_dv2 <- glm(
  ps.grad ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    non.english.home,
    family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv2
)

nobs(model1_dv2)
AIC(model1_dv2)

summary(model1_dv2)

exp(cbind(

    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
```

## Model 2: Demographics + High School Characteristics

This model adds high school contextual characteristics (district rurality, Economic Development Region, average county unemployment rate, and average county wages) to the demographic baseline from Model 1. N = 34,705.

**The likelihood ratio test confirms this block adds significant explanatory power** over Model 1, χ²(7) = 134.02, p \< .001. AIC improves from 42,739.24 to 42,619.21.

**District rurality shows a modest but significant association, with a notable non-linear pattern.** Students from **town/rural mix** districts (OR = 0.849, p \< .001) and **urban/town/rural mix** districts (OR = 0.790, p \< .001) both show lower odds of completion than entirely rural students, while **entirely urban** districts show no significant difference from entirely rural (OR = 0.923, p = .153). This is a different pattern than the workforce-attachment models, where entirely urban districts showed the largest, clearest effect — here it's the mixed-context districts that stand out.

**Economic Development Region shows a mixed picture.** **EDR 4 (West Central)** shows significantly higher odds of completion than EDR 1 (Northwest) (OR = 1.183, p \< .001), while **EDR 2 (Headwaters)** shows no significant difference (OR = 1.068, p = .197).

**Average county wages shows a strong, significant positive association** (OR = 2.654, p \< .001) — a notably large effect compared to the negligible practical magnitude this same variable showed in the earlier bivariate analysis against ps.grad. This is worth flagging directly: the bivariate estimate (essentially a raw mean-difference comparison) found this association to be statistically significant but "practically negligible" in size; here, in a multivariate context with other variables held constant, the odds ratio is considerably larger. This may reflect genuine confounding being resolved (other variables were masking a real wage effect) or a shift in what the coefficient represents once other high school characteristics and demographics are held fixed — worth a closer look at the variable's scale and distribution before drawing a strong substantive conclusion from this jump.

**Average county unemployment rate shows no significant association** (OR = 1.000, p = .967) — a departure from its consistent significance in both the workforce-attachment models and the earlier ps.grad bivariate analysis (which found avg.unemp.rate significant, unlike its non-significance for attended.ps and highest.cred.level).

**All demographic associations from Model 1 remain essentially unchanged**, both in direction and magnitude — gender, race/ethnicity (including the large Unknown category effect), economic status, special education status, and English learner status all show coefficients within a few hundredths of their Model 1 values. This indicates none of these demographic disparities in completion are explained by high school context.

**Model fit:** AIC = 42,619.21, residual deviance = 42,583 on 34,687 df, down from 42,717 on 34,694 df in Model 1.

**Summary:** High school context adds modest but significant explanatory power, driven primarily by district type (with mixed-context districts, not entirely urban ones, showing the clearest disadvantage) and by average county wages, which shows a considerably larger association here than its bivariate result suggested — worth further investigation before being taken at face value. Average county unemployment rate shows no association in this model, consistent with its non-significance in the earlier attended.ps and highest.cred.level bivariate work, though it had been significant in the ps.grad bivariate analysis specifically. All demographic disparities from Model 1 persist unchanged, indicating these are not explained by the high school context in which a student was educated.

```{r}
model2_dv2 <- glm(

)
```

## Model 3: Demographics + High School Characteristics + High School Accomplishments

This model adds high school accomplishment variables (PSEO participation, ACT participation and composite score, AP exam participation, and CTE achievement) to the demographics and high school characteristics blocks from Models 1–2. N = 34,705.

**The likelihood ratio test confirms this block adds significant explanatory power** over Model 2, χ²(6) = 3,653, p \< .001 — by far the largest single-block improvement in this sequence. AIC improves substantially, from 42,619.21 to 38,978.21.

**ACT participation shows a striking reversal from every workforce-attachment model examined so far — worth flagging directly.** Having taken the ACT is associated with **lower**, not higher, odds of postsecondary completion (OR = 0.731, p \< .001), while each additional point on the composite score is associated with **higher** odds (OR = 1.067, p \< .001). This is the opposite pattern from DV1a and DV1b, where taking the ACT strongly predicted *regional employment* while higher scores predicted *leaving* the region. Here, for completion itself, it's ACT score — not mere participation — that drives the positive academic-achievement story; simply sitting for the test without a correspondingly higher score is actually associated with lower completion odds, all else equal. This makes sense conceptually: the workforce models were capturing "did this person engage with the college-track pipeline at all," while this model is capturing "did they succeed within it" — different questions, appropriately different answers.

**PSEO participation shows a very strong positive association**, the largest accomplishment-related effect in this model. PSEO participants have roughly **99 percent higher odds** of completing postsecondary education (OR = 1.989, p \< .001), confirming PSEO's role as one of the strongest levers for completion identified throughout this project.

**AP exam participation is also strongly positive** (OR = 1.735, p \< .001), consistent with the bivariate finding that AP participants complete at meaningfully higher rates.

**CTE achievement, notably, shows no significant association with completion in this model** (both CTE Concentrator/Completer and CTE Participant categories are non-significant, p = .830 and p = .649) — a sharp contrast to CTE's strong, consistent, positive association with *regional workforce attachment* in both DV1a and DV1b. This confirms, in a fully controlled model, the pattern suggested throughout the bivariate work: CTE engagement is not really about whether someone completes postsecondary education at all — its value lies specifically in supporting regional workforce attachment, a different outcome entirely.

**Non-English home language flips to a significant positive association** in this model (OR = 1.305, p = .004), a change from essentially null in Models 1–2 (OR ≈ 0.98–1.00, non-significant). This emerging positive association, appearing only once accomplishments are controlled for, is worth a closer look — it may indicate that among students with similar accomplishment profiles, non-English home language is associated with somewhat higher completion, a pattern masked in the simpler models by correlation with other variables now held constant.

**Two high school characteristics shift direction or significance in this block.** District rurality's pattern changes: **entirely urban** districts now show significantly *higher* odds of completion (OR = 1.183, p = .006), a reversal from non-significance in Model 2, while urban/town/rural mix districts remain significantly lower (OR = 0.766, p \< .001). **EDR 2 (Headwaters)** becomes significantly *lower* than EDR 1 (OR = 0.761, p \< .001), a reversal from non-significance in Model 2. **Average county unemployment rate becomes significant and positive** (OR = 1.081, p \< .001), a change from non-significance in Model 2 — once accomplishments are accounted for, higher local unemployment is associated with higher odds of completion.

**All core demographic associations from Models 1–2 remain significant, though several attenuate somewhat in magnitude.** Special education status's effect shrinks considerably (OR = 0.545, up from OR = 0.266 in Models 1–2) — still a large, highly significant disadvantage, but roughly half its previous magnitude, indicating that accomplishments explain a substantial portion, though not all, of the special education completion gap. Economic status shows similar partial attenuation (OR = 0.514, up from OR = 0.397–0.393). The Unknown race/ethnicity category's extreme disadvantage also attenuates somewhat (OR = 0.163, up from OR = 0.085) but remains the largest racial/ethnic disparity in the model by a wide margin. American Indian, Black, and Hispanic disparities all persist with modest attenuation. Gender remains strongly significant and positive for women (OR = 1.442, down slightly from OR = 1.641).

**Model fit:** AIC = 38,978.21, residual deviance = 38,930 on 34,681 df, down substantially from 42,583 on 34,687 df in Model 2 — by far the best-fitting model in this sequence so far.

**Summary:** High school accomplishments dramatically improve model fit and reveal a clear divergence from the workforce-attachment models: for postsecondary completion, it's ACT *score* (not participation) and PSEO and AP participation that drive positive associations, while CTE achievement — so central to regional workforce attachment — shows no independent relationship with completion at all. This confirms, in a controlled model, that CTE functions as a distinct pathway oriented toward workforce entry rather than toward postsecondary completion itself. Accomplishments explain a meaningful share of the special education and economic status completion gaps, though both remain large and highly significant, and the profound Unknown race/ethnicity disparity — while somewhat attenuated — remains the single largest demographic effect in this model.


## DV2 Summary: What Predicts Postsecondary Completion (All High School Graduates)

This model sequence examined associations with postsecondary completion (ps.grad), modeled across the full graduating cohort regardless of postsecondary attendance (N = 34,705). Three models were fit sequentially — demographics, then high school characteristics, then high school accomplishments — with each block confirmed via likelihood ratio test to add significant explanatory power (all p \< .001). Model fit improved substantially across the sequence, from AIC = 42,739.24 (Model 1) to AIC = 38,978.21 (Model 3), with the accomplishments block producing by far the largest single improvement (a deviance reduction of 3,653 points from just six additional variables).

**The most striking finding of this sequence is that ACT participation and ACT composite score point in opposite directions for completion — the reverse of what both workforce-attachment models (DV1a, DV1b) showed.** Simply taking the ACT is associated with lower odds of completing postsecondary education (OR = 0.731, p \< .001), while each additional point on the composite score is associated with higher odds (OR = 1.067, p \< .001). This is a meaningful contrast with the workforce models, where ACT participation itself strongly predicted regional employment while higher scores predicted leaving the region. Here, for completion, it's demonstrated academic performance — not mere engagement with the test — that matters; participating without a correspondingly strong score is actually associated with somewhat lower completion odds, all else equal.

**PSEO participation and AP exam participation are the strongest positive accomplishment-related predictors of completion.** PSEO participants have roughly 99 percent higher odds of completing postsecondary education (OR = 1.989, p \< .001), and AP exam participants show a similarly strong positive association (OR = 1.735, p \< .001) — both confirming, in a fully controlled model, patterns that were among the strongest found throughout the earlier bivariate work.

**CTE achievement shows no significant association with completion whatsoever, a sharp and important divergence from its role in the workforce-attachment models.** Neither CTE concentrator/completer status nor CTE participation status is significant here (p = .830 and p = .649, respectively), in direct contrast to CTE's strong, consistent, positive relationship with regional workforce attachment throughout both DV1a and DV1b. This is a clean confirmation, now in a controlled multivariate model, of a pattern suggested repeatedly by the bivariate work: CTE engagement is not really about whether someone completes postsecondary education — its value lies specifically in supporting direct workforce attachment, a genuinely distinct outcome from completion itself.

**Demographic disparities are large, persistent, and only partially explained by high school context and accomplishments.** Special education status and economic status both show substantial disadvantages in completion that attenuate somewhat as accomplishments are added (special education status moving from OR = 0.266–0.267 in Models 1–2 to OR = 0.545 in Model 3; economic status moving from OR ≈ 0.393–0.398 to OR = 0.514) — indicating accomplishments explain a meaningful share of these gaps, but far from all of it, since both remain highly significant and substantial even in the final model. The Unknown race/ethnicity category shows an extreme disparity that also attenuates but remains the largest single effect in every model in this sequence (OR = 0.085 in Model 1, OR = 0.163 in Model 3) — students in this category are dramatically less likely to complete postsecondary education than any other group, a finding that has now surfaced consistently across the bivariate credential-level work and this fully controlled model, and likely warrants closer investigation into what this category actually represents in the data. American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students all show persistent, significant disadvantages relative to White students across all three models, with modest attenuation as context and accomplishments are added. Gender shows a large, stable, positive association throughout — women are consistently and substantially more likely than men to complete postsecondary education (OR = 1.442 in the final model).

**Non-English home language's association shifts from null to positive once accomplishments are controlled for** (from non-significant in Models 1–2 to OR = 1.305, p = .004, in Model 3) — worth a closer look, since this suggests that among students with comparable accomplishment profiles, non-English home language may be associated with somewhat higher completion, a relationship obscured in the simpler models.

**High school context shows a modest, somewhat shifting pattern across the sequence.** District rurality's relationship changes meaningfully once accomplishments are added: entirely urban districts move from non-significant (Model 2) to significantly higher completion odds (Model 3, OR = 1.183), while urban/town/rural mix districts remain significantly lower throughout. EDR 2 (Headwaters) similarly shifts from non-significant to significantly lower completion odds once accomplishments are accounted for. Average county wages shows a notably strong positive association in every model (OR ranging from 2.65–2.71) — considerably larger than the "practically negligible" magnitude this variable showed in the original bivariate analysis, a discrepancy worth further investigation before drawing firm substantive conclusions from the multivariate estimate. Average county unemployment rate moves from non-significant (Model 2) to significantly positive (Model 3, OR = 1.081).

**Overall Interpretation**

Taken together, this three-model sequence draws a clear line between what predicts postsecondary completion and what predicts regional workforce attachment — two outcomes that, throughout this project, have repeatedly pointed in different directions. Completion is driven by demonstrated academic achievement (ACT score, not mere participation), early college exposure (PSEO), and advanced coursework (AP) — the same academically-oriented profile that, in the workforce models, predicted leaving the region rather than staying. CTE engagement, meanwhile, shows no relationship with completion at all, reinforcing that its value operates through a distinct workforce-attachment channel rather than through the completion pipeline itself. Beneath these accomplishment-based patterns, persistent and substantial demographic disparities remain only partially explained by high school context and accomplishments — particularly the severe disadvantage associated with the Unknown race/ethnicity category, and the large, persistent gaps for special education status, economic disadvantage, and several racial/ethnic groups. These structural gaps appear to represent real, largely independent barriers to completion that are not resolved simply by improving access to accomplishment-building opportunities like PSEO or AP.

<br>

# Prep DV3 Data

Now we are focusing just on college completers. Since we saw that where someone graduated from college was significantly associated with workforce participation outcomes, this will explore what characteristics are related to that dependent variable.

```{r}

master.model.dv3 <- master %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2010,
         grad.year <= 2019,
         ps.grad == "Y",
         ps.grad.location != "Did not graduate ps",
         RaceEthnicity != "Unknown") %>%
  select(PersonID, all_of(final_ivs)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pseo.participant)) %>%
  mutate(ps.grad.location = ifelse(ps.grad.location == "PS grad region", "PS grad Region", "PS grad outside region"),
         ps.grad.location = fct_relevel(ps.grad.location, "PS grad outside region"),
    Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
    Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
    RaceEthnicity = fct_relevel(RaceEthnicity, "White"),
    economic.status = as_factor(economic.status),
    economic.status = fct_relevel(economic.status, "0"),
    SpecialEdStatus = as.character(SpecialEdStatus),
    SpecialEdStatus = fct_relevel(SpecialEdStatus, "0"),
    english.learner = as_factor(english.learner),
    english.learner = fct_relevel(english.learner, "0"),
    non.english.home = as_factor(non.english.home),
    non.english.home = fct_relevel(non.english.home, "0"),
    Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Entirely rural"),
    edr = fct_relevel(edr, "EDR 1 - Northwest"),
    pseo.participant = as.character(pseo.participant),
    pseo.participant = fct_relevel(pseo.participant, "0"),
    took.ACT = fct_relevel(took.ACT, "No"),
    ACTCompositeScore.filled = ifelse(is.na(ACTCompositeScore), 0, ACTCompositeScore),
    ap.exam = as_factor(ap.exam),
    ap.exam = fct_relevel(ap.exam, "0"),
    cte.achievement = fct_relevel(cte.achievement, "No CTE"))

```

# Modeling: College location - college completers only

## Model 1: Demographics

This baseline model examines demographic associations with graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region (vs. elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state), restricted to individuals who completed a postsecondary credential. N = 17,090.

**Special education status and economic status show the largest associations in this model, both in the direction of greater regional retention — consistent with the reversed pattern first identified in the bivariate `ps.grad.location` work.** Completers with special education status have roughly **91 percent higher odds** of graduating within the region (OR = 1.912, p \< .001), and economically disadvantaged completers have roughly **56 percent higher odds** (OR = 1.558, p \< .001). Both effects are large and highly significant, confirming in a multivariate setting what the bivariate analysis first suggested: among those who complete, disadvantage is associated with staying in the region rather than leaving.

**Race/ethnicity shows a mixed and, in one case, a striking pattern.** **American Indian completers have roughly 82 percent higher odds** of graduating within the region relative to White completers (OR = 1.816, p \< .001) — a large, clearly significant effect. **Asian/PI completers show the opposite pattern**, with roughly **44 percent lower odds** of in-region graduation (OR = 0.556, p = .001) — the only racial/ethnic group in this model significantly *less* likely to stay in the region. **Black and Hispanic completers show no significant difference** from White completers (p = .709 and p = .094, respectively).

**Non-English home language is associated with higher odds of in-region graduation** (OR = 1.508, p = .007), while **English learner status shows a marginal association in the opposite direction** (OR = 0.783, p = .071) — approaching but not reaching conventional significance. These two variables moving in different directions is worth noting, since they often move together in this analysis; it suggests home language and formal English learner classification may be capturing somewhat different populations with respect to regional retention specifically.

**Gender shows no significant association** with graduation location in this model (OR = 0.961, p = .211) — a contrast with its consistent significance in both the workforce-attachment and completion models examined earlier in this analysis.

**Model fit:** AIC = 23,143.95, residual deviance = 23,124 on 17,080 df (null deviance = 23,445 on 17,089 df).

**Summary:** At the demographics-only stage, this model confirms the reversed pattern first suggested by the bivariate work: economic disadvantage and special education status are both associated with substantially *higher* odds of regional retention among completers, not lower odds as seen for attendance, completion, and credential level. American Indian completers also show a notable regional-retention advantage, while Asian/PI completers show the opposite pattern — the only group significantly more likely to leave. As high school context and accomplishments are added in subsequent blocks, it will be important to watch whether these associations — particularly the large special education and economic status effects — hold or attenuate, especially given how the equivalent effects in the DV1b (workforce attachment) sequence fully attenuated once accomplishments were introduced.

```{r}
model1_dv3 <- glm(
  ps.grad.location ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    non.english.home,
  family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv3
)

summary(model1_dv3)
nobs(model1_dv3)
AIC(model1_dv3)
exp(cbind(OR = coef(model1_dv3), confint(model1_dv3)))

    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)

  )
```

## Model 2: Demographics + High School Characteristics

This model adds high school contextual characteristics (district rurality, Economic Development Region, average county unemployment rate, and average county wages) to the demographic baseline from Model 1. N = 17,090.

**The likelihood ratio test confirms this block adds significant explanatory power** over Model 1, χ²(7) = 101.04, p \< .001. AIC improves from 23,143.95 to 23,056.91.

**District rurality shows no significant association with in-region graduation in this model** — none of the three district-type categories differ significantly from entirely rural (all p \> .32). This is a different pattern from the workforce-attachment and completion models, where rurality showed consistent, often substantial effects; here, once demographics are accounted for, rurality doesn't distinguish where completers end up graduating.

**Economic Development Region shows a strong, significant association, and in a direction worth flagging.** Both **EDR 2 (Headwaters)** (OR = 0.671, p \< .001) and **EDR 4 (West Central)** (OR = 0.886, p = .005) show **lower** odds of in-region graduation relative to EDR 1 (Northwest). This means completers from EDR 1 specifically are the most likely to graduate within the region, while the other two EDRs show comparatively more outward mobility for postsecondary completion.

**Average county wages shows a strong, significant, negative association** (OR = 0.238, p \< .001) — higher local wages during high school are associated with substantially lower odds of graduating in-region. This is a notably large effect, and it moves in the opposite direction from what this variable showed in the completion model (DV2), where higher wages were associated with higher odds of completion generally. Combined, this suggests that in higher-wage areas, students are more likely to complete postsecondary education, but less likely to complete it within the region — worth keeping in mind as you interpret the coefficient practically, since the scale of avg.wages.pct.state should be double-checked given how large this odds ratio is relative to earlier bivariate findings on this variable.

**Average county unemployment rate remains significant and positive** (OR = 1.049, p \< .001), essentially unchanged from Model 1's pattern (unemployment rate wasn't included in Model 1 for this DV, so this is its first appearance — worth noting it enters significant immediately).

**All core demographic associations from Model 1 hold steady, both in direction and magnitude.** Special education status (OR = 1.952, up slightly from OR = 1.912) and economic status (OR = 1.558, essentially unchanged) both remain large, significant, and positive — the "reversed" pattern of disadvantage predicting regional retention persists after adding high school context. American Indian completers' regional-retention advantage remains strong and stable (OR = 1.769, essentially unchanged from OR = 1.816). Asian/PI completers' disadvantage also remains stable (OR = 0.557, essentially unchanged). Non-English home language remains significant and positive (OR = 1.441, down slightly from OR = 1.508). English learner status remains non-significant, and its coefficient moves slightly further from significance (p = .105, up from p = .071 in Model 1).

**Model fit:** AIC = 23,056.91, residual deviance = 23,023 on 17,073 df, down from 23,124 on 17,080 df in Model 1.

**Summary:** High school context adds modest but significant explanatory power, driven primarily by Economic Development Region and average county wages — both suggesting that completers from EDR 1 and from lower-wage counties are more likely to complete their credential within the region, while district rurality shows no independent association once demographics are held constant. All of the reversed demographic patterns established in Model 1 — economic disadvantage and special education status predicting greater regional retention, American Indian completers showing a retention advantage, Asian/PI completers showing the opposite — persist essentially unchanged through this block, suggesting these are not artifacts of the high school context completers came from.

```{r}

)
```

## Model 3: Demographics + High School Characteristics + High School Accomplishments

This model adds high school accomplishment variables (PSEO participation, ACT participation and composite score, AP exam participation, and CTE achievement) to the demographics and high school characteristics blocks from Models 1–2. N = 17,090.

**The likelihood ratio test confirms this block adds significant explanatory power** over Model 2, χ²(6) = 1,118.09, p \< .001 — by far the largest single-block improvement in this sequence. AIC improves substantially, from 23,056.91 to 21,950.82.

**ACT participation and composite score again show the divergent pattern that has run through this entire project, and here it's especially pronounced.** Having taken the ACT is associated with roughly **347 percent higher odds** of graduating within the region (OR = 4.470, p \< .001) — the largest coefficient in this entire model sequence — while each additional point on the composite score is associated with roughly **10 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.905, p \< .001), also a larger magnitude than seen in prior models. This confirms, in the sharpest terms yet, the pattern established earlier: engaging with the ACT strongly predicts staying local, while higher-scoring ACT-takers are progressively more likely to complete their credential elsewhere.

**AP exam participation is associated with lower odds of in-region graduation** (OR = 0.718, p \< .001), consistent with AP signaling the same academically-oriented, higher-mobility pathway as ACT score.

**CTE achievement shows a modest positive association**, in the expected direction given its role elsewhere in this analysis: CTE concentrators/completers show roughly 23 percent higher odds of in-region graduation (OR = 1.228, p \< .001), and CTE participants show a smaller but still significant 9 percent higher odds (OR = 1.089, p = .041) — smaller in magnitude here than CTE's effect on regional workforce attachment, but directionally consistent.

**PSEO participation is not significant in this model** (OR = 0.974, p = .480), a change from its strong positive role in the completion model (DV2) — suggesting PSEO's influence operates on *whether* someone completes, not *where*, once ACT and AP are accounted for.

**Two demographic associations attenuate meaningfully in this block, and one flips.** **Special education status drops to non-significance** (OR = 1.112, p = .185, down from OR = 1.952, p \< .001 in Model 2) — the large regional-retention advantage for special education completers established in Models 1–2 is substantially explained once accomplishments are accounted for. **American Indian completers' regional-retention advantage attenuates but remains significant** (OR = 1.481, down from OR = 1.769–1.816 in Models 1–2). **Economic status attenuates somewhat but remains strongly significant** (OR = 1.336, down from OR = 1.558) — a smaller, but still substantial, regional-retention advantage for economically disadvantaged completers persists even after accomplishments are controlled for.

**English learner status becomes significant and negative in this model** (OR = 0.670, p = .004), a change from non-significance in Models 1–2 (p = .071–.105) — once accomplishments are accounted for, English learner completers show meaningfully lower odds of in-region graduation.

**Asian/PI completers' disadvantage weakens slightly but remains significant** (OR = 0.599, p = .003, up from OR = 0.557 in Models 1–2). Black, Hispanic, and gender remain non-significant, consistent with prior models.

**High school context associations remain largely stable.** Average wages remains strongly negative and significant (OR = 0.232, essentially unchanged from Model 2). Average unemployment rate remains significant and positive, though its magnitude softens slightly (OR = 1.037, down from OR = 1.049). EDR 2's disadvantage weakens to marginal significance (OR = 0.865, p = .048, up from p \< .001 in Model 2), while EDR 4 becomes fully non-significant. District rurality shows a new significant effect: entirely urban districts now show significantly higher odds of in-region graduation (OR = 1.217, p = .014), a change from non-significance in Model 2.

**Model fit:** AIC = 21,950.82, residual deviance = 21,905 on 17,067 df, down substantially from 23,023 on 17,073 df in Model 2 — the best-fitting model in this sequence.

**Summary:** High school accomplishments dramatically improve model fit and produce the sharpest confirmation yet of this project's central tension: ACT participation strongly predicts staying local for postsecondary completion, while higher ACT scores and AP participation both predict completing elsewhere — the largest and most extreme version of this pattern found anywhere in this analysis. CTE achievement continues to show a modest, consistent, positive association with regional completion. Notably, the reversed demographic pattern established in Models 1–2 does not survive uniformly into this block: special education status's regional-retention advantage is substantially explained by accomplishments, while economic status's advantage attenuates but persists, and American Indian completers' advantage also persists in reduced form. English learner status shifts to a clear disadvantage once accomplishments are controlled for — the opposite of what a marginal Model 1–2 estimate might have suggested. Given how much movement is occurring across these three blocks, the demographic story for this outcome appears considerably more sensitive to specification than it was for the workforce-attachment or completion sequences.


## DV3 Summary: What Predicts Postsecondary Completion Within the Region (College Completers Only)

This model sequence examined associations with graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region (versus elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state), restricted to individuals who completed a postsecondary credential (N = 17,090). Three models were fit sequentially — demographics, then high school characteristics, then high school accomplishments — with each block confirmed via likelihood ratio test to add significant explanatory power (all p \< .001). Model fit improved substantially across the sequence, from AIC = 23,143.95 (Model 1) to AIC = 21,950.82 (Model 3), with the accomplishments block producing by far the largest single improvement.

**The sharpest and most extreme version of this project's central tension appears in this model sequence.** ACT participation is associated with roughly 347 percent higher odds of graduating within the region (OR = 4.470, p \< .001) — the single largest coefficient found in any model across this entire analysis — while each additional point on the composite score is associated with roughly 10 percent lower odds (OR = 0.905, p \< .001), also the largest magnitude seen for this effect anywhere in this project. AP exam participation reinforces the same pattern (OR = 0.718, p \< .001). Together, these confirm in the starkest terms yet that simply engaging with the ACT strongly predicts completing locally, while excelling on it — and pursuing advanced coursework generally — predicts completing elsewhere. CTE achievement, by contrast, shows a modest but consistent positive association with in-region completion (CTE concentrators/completers OR = 1.228, p \< .001), directionally aligned with CTE's role throughout this project, though smaller in magnitude here than its effect on regional workforce attachment.

**The demographic story for this outcome proved considerably more sensitive to model specification than for the other three dependent variables examined in this analysis.** In the demographics-only model, special education status and economic status both showed large, significant associations with greater regional retention among completers (OR = 1.912 and 1.558, respectively) — the same reversed pattern first identified in the earlier bivariate work. Special education status's advantage was **fully explained away** once accomplishments were introduced (dropping to OR = 1.112, non-significant, by Model 3) — paralleling what happened to the equivalent effect in the workforce-attachment sequence. Economic status's advantage attenuated but **persisted** through the full sequence (OR = 1.336 in the final model, still highly significant) — a genuine, independent relationship between economic disadvantage and regional completion that survives full controls, unlike the workforce-attachment sequence where this association fully disappeared.

**Race/ethnicity showed a distinctive pattern for this outcome, unlike anything seen in the other three dependent variables.** American Indian completers consistently showed the **largest positive** racial/ethnic association with regional retention across every model (OR = 1.481 in the final model, attenuating from OR = 1.816–1.769 in Models 1–2, but remaining significant throughout) — the opposite direction from the workforce-attachment and completion models, where American Indian students showed no advantage or a modest disadvantage. Asian/PI completers showed the reverse pattern throughout — significantly **lower** odds of in-region completion in every model (OR = 0.599 in the final model) — the only racial/ethnic group consistently associated with leaving the region for postsecondary completion. Black and Hispanic completers showed no significant association with graduation location in any model in this sequence.

**English learner status showed an unusual trajectory across this sequence, moving from a marginal, borderline association to a clear and significant disadvantage only once accomplishments were introduced** (from p = .071–.105 in Models 1–2 to OR = 0.670, p = .004, in Model 3) — indicating that once academic accomplishment differences are held constant, English learner completers are meaningfully less likely to complete their credential within the region.

**High school context showed a mixed pattern, with wage level standing out as the strongest and most stable contextual effect in this entire sequence.** Average county wages showed a large, consistent, negative association with in-region completion across all three models (OR ranging from 0.232–0.238) — students from higher-wage counties were substantially more likely to complete elsewhere, the opposite direction from this variable's positive relationship with completion generally in DV2. This divergence is worth flagging: higher local wages appear to support completion overall while simultaneously predicting outward mobility for where that completion happens. Average county unemployment rate remained modestly positive and significant throughout. Economic Development Region showed EDR 1 (Northwest) as consistently associated with the highest in-region completion rates relative to the other two EDRs, though this association weakened as accomplishments were added. District rurality showed no consistent pattern until the final model, where entirely urban districts emerged as significantly more likely to complete in-region.

**Overall Interpretation**

Taken together, this three-model sequence confirms, in its most extreme form anywhere in this analysis, the core tension between academic achievement and geographic mobility that has defined this entire project: ACT engagement predicts staying local, while ACT performance and AP participation both predict leaving. What sets this outcome apart from the workforce-attachment and completion sequences is the degree to which the demographic story shifted across blocks — economic disadvantage's association with regional retention proved genuinely independent of accomplishments (unlike special education status, whose association was fully explained by them), and race/ethnicity revealed a distinctive pattern, with American Indian completers most likely and Asian/PI completers least likely to complete their credential within the region, holding all else constant. The unexpected negative relationship between county wage level and in-region completion — running opposite to this variable's positive relationship with completion overall — suggests that local economic conditions shape not just whether students complete postsecondary education, but distinctly influence where they choose or are able to complete it, a nuance not captured by the other three dependent variables in this analysis.

<br>

# Prep DV4 Data

Another post-secondary independent variable that was strongly associated with workforce participation outcomes was the highest credential earned by an individual. This analysis will explore what characteristics are associated with earned credentials.

```{r}
master.model.dv4 <- master %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2010,
         grad.year <= 2019,
         ps.grad == "Y",
         highest.cred.level != "Did not graduate ps",
         RaceEthnicity != "Unknown") %>%
  select(PersonID, all_of(final_ivs)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pseo.participant)) %>%
  mutate(highest.cred.level = ifelse(highest.cred.level %in% c("Associate degree", "Less than Associate Degree"), "Associate or lesser credential", highest.cred.level),
         highest.cred.level = fct_relevel(highest.cred.level, "Bachelor degree or higher"),
         Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
         Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
         RaceEthnicity = fct_relevel(RaceEthnicity, "White"),
         economic.status = as_factor(economic.status),
         economic.status = fct_relevel(economic.status, "0"),
         SpecialEdStatus = as.character(SpecialEdStatus),
         SpecialEdStatus = fct_relevel(SpecialEdStatus, "0"),
         english.learner = as_factor(english.learner),
         english.learner = fct_relevel(english.learner, "0"),
         non.english.home = as_factor(non.english.home),
         non.english.home = fct_relevel(non.english.home, "0"),
         Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Entirely rural"),
         edr = fct_relevel(edr, "EDR 1 - Northwest"),
         pseo.participant = as.character(pseo.participant),
         pseo.participant = fct_relevel(pseo.participant, "0"),
         took.ACT = fct_relevel(took.ACT, "No"),
         ACTCompositeScore.filled = ifelse(is.na(ACTCompositeScore), 0, ACTCompositeScore),
         ap.exam = as_factor(ap.exam),
         ap.exam = fct_relevel(ap.exam, "0"),
         cte.achievement = fct_relevel(cte.achievement, "No CTE"))

```

# Modeling: Credential Earned - college completers only

## Model 1: Demographics

This baseline model examines demographic associations with earning a sub-baccalaureate credential (associate degree or less) versus a bachelor's degree or higher, restricted to individuals who completed a postsecondary credential. N = 17,129.

**Special education status shows by far the largest association in this model.** Completers with special education status have roughly **386 percent higher odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential rather than a bachelor's degree (OR = 4.861, p \< .001) — the largest single effect found anywhere in this analysis to date, confirming and sharpening the disparity already identified in the earlier bivariate credential-level work.

**Economic status shows a similarly large, though smaller, effect.** Economically disadvantaged completers have roughly **101 percent higher odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential (OR = 2.015, p \< .001) — a substantial disparity, consistent with the direction and general magnitude found in the bivariate analysis.

**Gender shows a strong, significant association, with women considerably more likely to earn a bachelor's degree.** Women have roughly **36 percent lower odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential relative to men (OR = 0.645, p \< .001) — i.e., substantially higher odds of reaching the bachelor's level, consistent with the gender pattern found in the bivariate work and in the completion model (DV2), where women were also more likely to complete postsecondary education overall.

**Race/ethnicity shows a mixed pattern.** **American Indian completers have roughly 53 percent higher odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential relative to White completers (OR = 1.534, p \< .001). **Asian/PI completers show the opposite pattern**, with roughly **46 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.541, p = .001) — i.e., Asian/PI completers are considerably more likely to reach the bachelor's level. **Hispanic completers show a modest, marginally significant association toward sub-baccalaureate credentials** (OR = 1.307, p = .049). **Black completers show no significant difference** from White completers (p = .743).

**English learner status and non-English home language point in opposite directions, worth flagging directly.** English learner completers have roughly **86 percent higher odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential (OR = 1.857, p \< .001), while completers from non-English-speaking homes have roughly **35 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.648, p = .010) — i.e., more likely to reach the bachelor's level. These two related-but-distinct variables moving in opposite directions echoes a similar divergence seen in the DV3 model (graduation location), where these two variables also failed to move together — suggesting formal English learner classification and home language capture meaningfully different populations with respect to postsecondary outcomes.

**Model fit:** AIC = 21,047.86, residual deviance = 21,028 on 17,119 df (null deviance = 22,211 on 17,128 df).

**Summary:** At the demographics-only stage, special education status and economic disadvantage show the largest associations with earning a sub-baccalaureate rather than a bachelor's credential, both substantially larger in magnitude than any comparable effect seen for the completion (DV2) or graduation-location (DV3) outcomes. Gender, race/ethnicity, and language-related factors all show significant associations as well, with English learner status and non-English home language notably diverging in direction. As high school context and accomplishments are added in subsequent blocks, it will be worth watching whether these large demographic effects — particularly special education status — attenuate substantially, as similar effects did in the workforce-attachment sequences, or whether they persist as more durable, independent associations.

```{r}
model1_dv4 <- glm(
  highest.cred.level ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    non.english.home,
  family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv4
)

summary(model1_dv4)
nobs(model1_dv4)
AIC(model1_dv4)

exp(cbind(OR = coef(model1_dv4), confint(model1_dv4)))

or_plot <- tidy(model1_dv4, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Make labels nicer (edit these replacements to match your exact factor labels)
    term = str_replace_all(term, c(
      "RaceEthnicity" = "Race: ",
      "economic.status" = "Economic status: ",
      "SpecialEdStatus" = "Special Ed: ",
      "pseo.participant" = "PSEO: ",
      "cte.achievement" = "CTE: ",
      "MCA.M" = "MCA Math",
      "highest.cred.level" = "Highest credential"
    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
             color = "grey85") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
    labels = c("0.5", "0.75", "1.0", "1.25", "1.5", "2.0")
  ) +
  theme_line +
  labs(
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL
  )
```

<br>

## Model 2: Demographics + High School Characteristics

This model adds high school contextual characteristics (district rurality, Economic Development Region, average county unemployment rate, and average county wages) to the demographic baseline from Model 1. N = 17,129.

**The likelihood ratio test confirms this block adds significant explanatory power** over Model 1, χ²(7) = 145.49, p \< .001. AIC improves from 21,047.86 to 20,916.37.

**District rurality shows a clear, significant pattern in this model.** Completers from **entirely urban** districts have roughly **35 percent lower odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential relative to entirely rural completers (OR = 0.655, p \< .001) — i.e., urban completers are considerably more likely to reach the bachelor's level. **Urban/town/rural mix** districts show a similar, somewhat smaller pattern (OR = 0.764, p \< .001). **Town/rural mix** districts show no significant difference from entirely rural.

**Economic Development Region shows a strong, significant association, with both EDR 2 and EDR 4 associated with lower odds of sub-baccalaureate attainment relative to EDR 1.** **EDR 2 (Headwaters)** completers have roughly **42 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.576, p \< .001), and **EDR 4 (West Central)** completers have roughly **11 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.889, p = .009) — meaning EDR 1 completers are the most likely to earn a sub-baccalaureate credential rather than a bachelor's degree, a notably large gap for EDR 2 specifically.

**Average county unemployment rate remains significant and positive** (OR = 1.045, p \< .001): higher local unemployment during high school is associated with modestly higher odds of sub-baccalaureate attainment.

**Average county wages shows no significant association** (OR = 1.058, p = .819).

**All core demographic associations from Model 1 hold essentially steady.** Special education status (OR = 4.833, essentially unchanged from OR = 4.861) and economic status (OR = 2.009, essentially unchanged from OR = 2.015) both remain the largest and most stable effects in this model, confirming these are not explained by high school context. Gender remains strongly significant and stable (OR = 0.645). American Indian completers' association with sub-baccalaureate attainment strengthens somewhat (OR = 1.788, up from OR = 1.534), while Asian/PI completers' association toward bachelor's attainment remains stable (OR = 0.531). **Hispanic ethnicity drops to non-significance** (OR = 1.225, p = .138, down from p = .049 in Model 1) — its modest Model 1 association appears to have been partly explained by high school context. Non-English home language remains significant (OR = 0.697, p = .033, similar magnitude to Model 1). English learner status remains significant and strengthens slightly (OR = 1.900, up from OR = 1.857).

**Model fit:** AIC = 20,916.37, residual deviance = 20,882 on 17,112 df, down from 21,028 on 17,119 df in Model 1.

**Summary:** High school context adds meaningful explanatory power, driven by district rurality and Economic Development Region — both showing that completers from urban districts and from EDR 2 specifically are considerably more likely to reach the bachelor's level, while local unemployment rate shows a small positive association with sub-baccalaureate attainment. The two largest demographic associations from Model 1 — special education status and economic status — remain essentially unchanged, confirming these represent durable, context-independent disparities in credential level. Hispanic ethnicity's modest Model 1 association attenuates to non-significance, suggesting it was partly a function of high school context rather than an independent effect.

```{r}
model2_dv4 <- glm(
  highest.cred.level ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    non.english.home +
    Dem_Desc +
    edr +
    avg.wages.pct.state +
    avg.unemp.rate,
  family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv4
)

summary(model2_dv4)

nobs(model1_dv4)
nobs(model2_dv4)

AIC(model1_dv4)
AIC(model2_dv4)

exp(cbind(OR = coef(model2_dv4), confint(model2_dv4)))

anova(model1_dv4, model2_dv4, test = "Chisq")


or_plot <- tidy(model2_dv4, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Make labels nicer (edit these replacements to match your exact factor labels)
    term = str_replace_all(term, c(
      "RaceEthnicity" = "Race: ",
      "economic.status" = "Economic status: ",
      "SpecialEdStatus" = "Special Ed: ",
      "pseo.participant" = "PSEO: ",
      "cte.achievement" = "CTE: ",
      "MCA.M" = "MCA Math",
      "highest.cred.level" = "Highest credential"
    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
             color = "grey85") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
    labels = c("0.5", "0.75", "1.0", "1.25", "1.5", "2.0")
  ) +
  theme_line +
  labs(
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL
  )
```

## Model 3: Demographics + High School Characteristics + High School Accomplishments

This model adds high school accomplishment variables (PSEO participation, ACT participation and composite score, AP exam participation, and CTE achievement) to the demographics and high school characteristics blocks from Models 1–2. N = 17,129.

**The likelihood ratio test confirms this block adds significant explanatory power** over Model 2, χ²(6) = 3,963.3, p \< .001 — by far the largest single-block improvement in this sequence, and one of the largest improvements found anywhere across this entire analysis. AIC drops sharply, from 20,916.37 to 16,965.10.

**ACT participation shows the largest coefficient found anywhere in this entire analysis.** Having taken the ACT is associated with roughly **1,220 percent higher odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential rather than a bachelor's degree (OR = 13.204, p \< .001). At the same time, each additional point on the composite score is associated with roughly **18 percent lower odds** (OR = 0.823, p \< .001) — also one of the larger score-based effects in this analysis. Together, these represent the most extreme version yet of the pattern running throughout this project: taking the ACT strongly predicts a sub-baccalaureate outcome, while scoring well on it strongly predicts reaching the bachelor's level instead.

**AP exam participation shows a strong association toward bachelor's attainment** (OR = 0.510, p \< .001) — AP participants are roughly half as likely to earn a sub-baccalaureate credential relative to a bachelor's degree, consistent with AP's role throughout this analysis as a marker of the academically-oriented pathway.

**PSEO participation also shows a strong association toward bachelor's attainment** (OR = 0.596, p \< .001) — a different role than PSEO played in the graduation-location model (DV3), where it was non-significant, but consistent with its strong role in the completion model (DV2).

**CTE achievement shows a strong, significant association toward sub-baccalaureate credentials, the largest CTE effect found in any model in this analysis.** CTE concentrators/completers have roughly **84 percent higher odds** of earning a sub-baccalaureate credential (OR = 1.836, p \< .001), and CTE participants show a smaller but significant 16 percent higher odds (OR = 1.156, p = .004) — confirming CTE's consistent association with the sub-baccalaureate/regional-workforce-oriented pathway, now shown directly for credential level itself.

**Non-English home language shows a strong, significant association toward bachelor's attainment** (OR = 0.475, p \< .001), strengthening from Model 2 (OR = 0.697) — completers from non-English-speaking homes are considerably more likely to reach the bachelor's level once accomplishments are accounted for.

**Several demographic associations attenuate substantially in this block.** **Special education status's effect drops sharply** (OR = 1.498, down from OR = 4.833 in Model 2) — still significant, but explaining away roughly two-thirds of its previous magnitude, indicating that much (though not all) of the special education credential-level gap operates through accomplishment differences (particularly ACT participation) rather than reflecting an independent disadvantage. **Economic status attenuates similarly, though less dramatically** (OR = 1.576, down from OR = 2.009) — a substantial but still significant disadvantage persists. **American Indian completers' association drops to marginal non-significance** (OR = 1.242, p = .082, down from OR = 1.788, p \< .001 in Model 2) — largely explained by accomplishments. **Asian/PI completers' association toward bachelor's attainment remains stable** (OR = 0.519, essentially unchanged). **Black completers show a newly marginal association** (OR = 0.727, p = .097) toward bachelor's attainment, a shift from non-significance in Models 1–2.

**English learner status drops to marginal non-significance** (OR = 1.335, p = .096, down from OR = 1.900, p \< .001 in Model 2) — its earlier strong association appears substantially explained by accomplishments.

**Gender remains significant and strengthens somewhat** (OR = 0.752, down from OR = 0.645–0.645 in Models 1–2, indicating a smaller — though still substantial — gap once accomplishments are accounted for).

**High school context shows some notable shifts.** Average county unemployment rate becomes non-significant (OR = 0.996, p = .789), a change from significant in Models 1–2. EDR 2's disadvantage (association with sub-baccalaureate attainment) becomes non-significant (p = .673), while EDR 4 flips to a significant *positive* association with sub-baccalaureate attainment (OR = 1.162, p = .004) — a reversal from its Model 2 direction. District rurality remains significant across all three categories, essentially stable in direction from Model 2.

**Model fit:** AIC = 16,965.10, residual deviance = 16,919 on 17,106 df, down dramatically from 20,882 on 17,112 df in Model 2 — by far the best-fitting model in this sequence, and the largest fit improvement of any block across this entire analysis.

**Summary:** High school accomplishments produce the largest and most dramatic model improvement found anywhere in this analysis, and reveal the single largest coefficient of the entire project: ACT participation is associated with more than a twelve-fold increase in the odds of earning a sub-baccalaureate rather than a bachelor's credential, while ACT score, AP participation, and PSEO participation all point toward bachelor's attainment instead — the clearest and most extreme confirmation of the academic-achievement-versus-credential-type tension found anywhere in this project. CTE achievement shows its strongest association with sub-baccalaureate attainment of any model examined. Meanwhile, the large special education and economic status disparities established in Models 1–2 both attenuate substantially — though economic status remains clearly significant while special education status, while still significant, loses roughly two-thirds of its prior magnitude — indicating these accomplishment variables explain a meaningful share, though not all, of the underlying demographic gaps in credential level.

```{r}
model3_dv4 <- glm(
  highest.cred.level ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    non.english.home +
    Dem_Desc +
    edr +
    avg.wages.pct.state +
    avg.unemp.rate +
    pseo.participant +
    took.ACT +
    ACTCompositeScore.filled +
    ap.exam + 
    cte.achievement,
    family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv4
)

summary(model3_dv4)

nobs(model1_dv4)
nobs(model2_dv4)
nobs(model3_dv4)

AIC(model1_dv4)
AIC(model2_dv4)
AIC(model3_dv4)

anova(model1_dv4, model2_dv4, model3_dv4, test = "Chisq")

  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Make labels nicer (edit these replacements to match your exact factor labels)
    term = str_replace_all(term, c(
      "RaceEthnicity" = "Race: ",
      "economic.status" = "Economic status: ",
      "SpecialEdStatus" = "Special Ed: ",
      "pseo.participant" = "PSEO: ",
      "cte.achievement" = "CTE: ",
      "MCA.M" = "MCA Math",
      "highest.cred.level" = "Highest credential"
    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
             color = "grey85") +
  geom_point() +

    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",

  ) +

    breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2),

  ) +

    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
```
